propositions.text: Applicant is from Burundi and left in June 2008 to the US with a Burundian passport under the name Deria Girukwishaka.
propositions.quote: The applicant is from Burundi. In June 2008, she left Burundi to go to the United States on the pretext of participating in a student exchange with the Global Youth Institute in Iowa. At the time, she had a U.S. visa and a Burundian passport issued in the name of Deria Girukwishaka, born on November 23, 1990.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant is from Burundi and left for the US in June 2008 with a Burundian passport under the name Deria Girukwishaka, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant entered Canada July 22, 2008, claiming refugee protection as Deria Uwitonze with three identity documents in that name.
propositions.quote: On July 22, 2008, she entered Canada and claimed refugee protection under the name Deria Uwitonze, born on January 23, 1990. She provided three (3) identity documents in this name: a Burundian national identity card, a Burundian student card and a birth certificate.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant entered Canada July 22, 2008, claiming refugee protection as Deria Uwitonze with three identity documents, court states.

propositions.text: On July 25, 2008, CBSA officer questioned applicant who said her Deria Girukwishaka passport was stolen; she was then detained.
propositions.quote: Questioned by a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officer on July 25, 2008, the applicant stated that the passport in the name of Deria Girukwishaka was stolen in New York. She was then arrested and detained pending identification.

paragraphs.summary: On July 25, 2008, CBSA questioned applicant who said her passport was stolen; she was detained, court states.

propositions.text: While in custody, CBSA counterfeit analyst found no significant alteration but analysis inconclusive without comparison specimen.
propositions.quote: While the applicant was in custody, a CBSA counterfeit analyst produced an expert report on the three (3) identity documents submitted by the applicant. On August 4, 2008, the analyst found that the three (3) documents did not contain “any significant signs of alteration,” but that the results of the analysis were “inconclusive” in the absence of a comparison specimen.

paragraphs.summary: While in custody, CBSA analyst found no significant alteration but analysis inconclusive without comparison specimen, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant was conditionally released August 18, 2008, without true identity determined.
propositions.quote: On August 18, 2008, the applicant was placed on conditional release without her true identity having been determined.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was conditionally released August 18, 2008, without true identity determined, court states.

propositions.text: RPD rejected refugee claim May 10, 2011, found applicant not credible and true identity was Deria Girukwishaka.
propositions.quote: On May 10, 2011, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected her refugee claim. It did not find the applicant’s testimony credible, including with respect to the price and procedures for obtaining a Burundian identity card. While acknowledging that she was a Burundian national, the RPD found that the applicant’s true identity was Deria Girukwishaka, not Deria Uwitonze.

propositions.text: Judicial review of RPD decision dismissed by this Court January 17, 2012.
propositions.quote: An application for judicial review of this decision was dismissed by this Court on January 17, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: RPD rejected refugee claim May 2011, found applicant not credible and true identity was Deria Girukwishaka; judicial review dismissed January 2012, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant filed permanent residence application on humanitarian grounds November 2011, allowed in first step March 2013 after producing more documents.
propositions.quote: In November 2011, the applicant filed an application for permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Her application was allowed in the first step of the process in March 2013. In order to confirm that her identity was actually Deria Uwitonze, she produced several other documents including a laissez-passer replacing a passport issued by the Embassy of Burundi in Canada, school report cards, a certificate of family composition and several affidavits.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant filed permanent residence application November 2011, allowed first step March 2013 after producing more documents, court states.

propositions.text: Immigration officer denied application July 20, 2016, for failure to prove identity conclusively and missing prescribed documents under IRPR.
propositions.quote: On July 20, 2016, an immigration officer denied the application on the basis that the applicant failed to prove her identity conclusively and because she did not submit prescribed documents pursuant to subsection 50(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (IRPR).

paragraphs.summary: Immigration officer denied application July 20, 2016, for failure to prove identity conclusively and missing prescribed documents, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of the immigration officer's decision.
propositions.quote: The applicant is seeking judicial review of this decision.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of immigration officer's decision, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant claims immigration officer's decision was unreasonable, violated natural justice, and was biased.
propositions.quote: The applicant claims that the immigration officer’s decision was unreasonable and in violation of the rules of natural justice. She also criticizes the officer for being biased.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant claims immigration officer's decision was unreasonable, violated natural justice, and was biased, applicant argues.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is standard for reviewing immigration officer's humanitarian and compassionate relief decisions (Kanthasamy).
propositions.quote: It is well established that reasonableness is the standard for reviewing an immigration officer’s decision to grant relief on humanitarian and compassionate grounds (Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at para. 44).

propositions.text: Assessment of identity, evidence evaluation, and prescribed document determination are within immigration officer's jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: The assessment of the applicant’s identity, the evaluation of the evidence and the determination of what constitutes a prescribed document within the meaning of subsection 50(1) of the IRPR raise either questions of fact, mixed questions of fact and law or questions of law within the jurisdiction of an immigration officer (Demiri v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 1104 at para. 12; Andryanov v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 186 at para. 14).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness is standard for reviewing immigration officer's humanitarian relief decisions; identity and evidence assessment are within officer's jurisdiction, court states.

propositions.text: Correctness standard applies to natural justice or bias issues (Khosa; Khela).
propositions.quote: However, when issues of natural justice or procedural fairness are involved, including those involving allegations of bias, the more stringent standard of correctness must be applied (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para. 43; Mission Institution v. Khela, 2014 SCC 24 at para. 79).

propositions.text: Question is whether decision-maker's process was fair, not whether decision was correct (Majdalani).
propositions.quote: The question in this case is not really whether the decision was “correct,” but rather whether the process followed by the decision-maker was fair (Majdalani v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 294 at para. 15).

paragraphs.summary: Correctness standard applies to natural justice or bias issues; question is whether process was fair, court states.

propositions.text: Only one argument is needed to dispose of judicial review; court will not rule on others.
propositions.quote: Although the applicant raised several arguments, only one is needed to dispose of this application for judicial review. As a result, the Court does not intend to rule on the other arguments.

paragraphs.summary: Court will dispose of judicial review on one argument and not rule on others, court states.

propositions.text: Officer noted counterfeit analyst's inconclusive report due to no comparison specimen.
propositions.quote: In her decision, the officer noted that the applicant’s national identity card was analyzed by a counterfeit analyst and that the results of the analysis were inconclusive because there was no comparison specimen.

propositions.text: Officer observed date of birth erased on original document, concluded document altered.
propositions.quote: The officer then indicated that she examined the original document and observed that the date of birth was erased and that this correction was clearly visible on the copy. Her observations led her to conclude that the document had been altered.

propositions.text: Officer found national identity card number same as brother's card issued two years earlier, doubted authenticity.
propositions.quote: She also noted that the applicant’s national identity card bore the same number as the one on her brother’s national identity card issued two (2) years earlier. The officer found that it was unlikely, on a preponderance of the evidence, that the two (2) cards would bear the same number, and therefore asserted that the authenticity of the national identity card was dubious.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted inconclusive analyst report, observed erased date of birth, and found identity card number same as brother's, doubting authenticity, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: Applicant argues officer failed to inform her of doubts about identity card alteration and should have allowed response.
propositions.quote: The applicant criticized the officer for not having told her that she had doubts as to whether the national identity card might have been altered. She contended that the officer should have given her the opportunity to answer her questions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues officer failed to inform her of doubts about identity card alteration and should have allowed response, applicant says.

propositions.text: Respondent argues officer had no obligation to inform applicant of doubts and applicant knew of doubts from CBSA officer.
propositions.quote: The respondent argued that the officer was under no obligation to inform the applicant of her doubts. He pointed out that the applicant was aware that the authenticity of her national identity card raised doubts since the CBSA officer at the port of entry had also noted that the date of birth appeared to have been changed.

propositions.text: Respondent says officer could see document altered despite expert report and applicant had burden to prove identity.
propositions.quote: The respondent added that the officer could certainly see that the document in question had been altered, notwithstanding the findings of the expert report completed by the CBSA’s counterfeit analyst. Finally, the respondent argued that the applicant had the burden of proving her identity and could see that the document had been corrected and that the numbering was identical on the two (2) cards.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues officer had no duty to inform applicant of doubts, applicant knew from CBSA officer, and applicant had burden to prove identity, respondent says.

propositions.text: Applicant must provide convincing evidence to confirm identity; officer not required to notify inadequacies or provide opportunity to dispel doubts if evidence insufficient.
propositions.quote: The Court agrees with the respondent that it is incumbent upon the applicant to provide the officer with convincing evidence to confirm her identity (Lhamo v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 873 at para. 28; Bah v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 14 at para. 33). The officer is not required to notify the applicant of inadequacies in her application nor in the material provided in support of the application (De La Cruz Garcia v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 784 at para. 12). Nor is she required to provide the applicant with an opportunity to dispel any doubts or concerns when the material provided in support of her application is unclear, incomplete or insufficient (Rani v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1414 at para. 17 [Rani]; Kuhathasan v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 457 at para. 37 [Kuhathasan]; Hassani v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1283 at para. 24).

paragraphs.summary: Court states applicant must provide convincing evidence; officer not required to notify inadequacies or allow dispelling doubts if evidence insufficient.

propositions.text: If officer doubts credibility or authenticity of applicant's information or documents, officer must inform applicant and allow response.
propositions.quote: However, it is well established that where an immigration officer’s doubts involve the credibility, accuracy or authenticity of the information provided by an applicant in support of her application, including the authenticity of documents produced by an applicant, the immigration officer must inform the applicant and give her an opportunity to address them (Mursalim v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 264 at para. 16; Rani at para. 18; Kuhathasan at para. 37).

paragraphs.summary: Court states officer must inform applicant and allow response if doubts involve credibility or authenticity of information or documents.

propositions.text: Court finds officer should have informed applicant of doubts about national identity card authenticity and allowed response.
propositions.quote: The Court is of the view that in the circumstances of this case, the officer should have informed the applicant of the doubts she had with respect to the authenticity of her national identity card and given her the opportunity to address them.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds officer should have informed applicant of doubts about identity card authenticity and allowed response.

propositions.text: Respondent argues CBSA officer questioned applicant about identity card date of birth change on July 25, 2008.
propositions.quote: The Court recognizes, as the respondent argues, that the CBSA officer at the port of entry questioned the applicant about her identity card on July 25, 2008, the date on which the applicant was detained pending identification. The officer asked her why the date of birth on the identification document appeared to have been changed.

propositions.text: Applicant replied she did not know why date of birth was changed and said she got card at Bujumbura city hall maybe the year before.
propositions.quote: The applicant replied that she did not know and that she went to get it at the Bujumbura city hall “maybe” the year before.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues CBSA officer questioned applicant about identity card date change July 25, 2008; applicant replied she did not know and got card maybe year before.

propositions.text: The counterfeit expert assessment results were not questioned by the RPD in its decision.
propositions.quote: the counterfeit expert assessment ordered on July 29, 2008, the results of which were verbally communicated to the applicant while she was in detention, was not called into question by the RPD in its decision.

propositions.text: The RPD's finding on the national identity card was based on applicant's lack of knowledge of price and procedure for obtaining it.
propositions.quote: the RPD’s finding with respect to the national identity card was based on the applicant’s lack of knowledge of the price and procedure for obtaining such a card.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the applicant to believe issues about alteration of her identity card were no longer a concern when applying for permanent residence.
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the applicant to believe that the issues involving the alteration of her identity card were no longer a concern when she made representations regarding her application for permanent residence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not question the counterfeit expert assessment and based its finding on applicant's lack of knowledge; applicant reasonably believed identity card issues were resolved.

propositions.text: No indication the officer raised concerns about identical numbering on applicant's and brother's identity cards to applicant for explanation.
propositions.quote: there is no indication that this concern was raised with the applicant in order to give her an opportunity to provide an explanation in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no indication the officer gave the applicant a chance to explain concerns about identical numbering on identity cards.

propositions.text: Officer communicated concerns about school report cards via fairness letter and interview opportunity.
propositions.quote: On March 10, 2016, the officer sent the applicant a fairness letter containing the results of the verification of her school report cards and called her for an interview on April 1, 2016, to give her an opportunity to provide an explanation in this regard.

propositions.text: Fairness letter did not mention concerns about national identity card or doubts about its authenticity.
propositions.quote: The fairness letter makes no mention of the officer’s concerns about the national identity card or of her doubts as to its authenticity.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer gave a fairness letter and interview for school report cards but did not mention concerns about the national identity card.

propositions.text: Officer's finding on authenticity of national identity card gave rise to procedural fairness obligation.
propositions.quote: The Court is of the opinion that the officer’s finding as to the authenticity of the applicant’s national identity card gave rise to the obligation of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Officer should have given applicant reasonable opportunity to respond to doubts about identity card authenticity.
propositions.quote: The officer should have given the applicant a reasonable opportunity to respond to the doubts she had about the authenticity of the national identity card.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the officer had a procedural fairness duty and should have let the applicant respond to doubts about her identity card.

propositions.text: Breach of procedural fairness is significant because officer's decision partly based on doubtful authenticity of identity card.
propositions.quote: The Court further considers the breach of procedural fairness in this case to be significant. The officer’s finding that the laissez-passer replacing a passport is not a prescribed document under subsection 50(1) of the IRPR is based, at least in part, on the fact that the laissez-passer was obtained with the applicant’s national identity card, the authenticity of which is in doubt.

propositions.text: It is impossible to know if officer's decision would differ if doubts about identity card were dispelled.
propositions.quote: It is impossible for the Court to know whether the officer’s decision would have been different had her doubts about the identity card been dispelled.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the procedural fairness breach significant as the officer's decision partly relied on doubtful identity card authenticity; outcome uncertain.

propositions.text: Officer's decision on identity card authenticity is unreasonable for lacking transparency, justification, intelligibility per Dunsmuir.
propositions.quote: the officer’s decision regarding the authenticity of the national identity card is also unreasonable because it lacks transparency, justification and intelligibility, according to the requirements set out in Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9.

propositions.text: Officer failed to specify expert's assertion that microscope and spectral comparator found no significant signs of alteration.
propositions.quote: the officer failed to specify that the expert also asserted that the examination of the identity card with a microscope and a video spectral comparator did not reveal any significant signs of alteration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer's decision unreasonable and lacking transparency, failing to mention expert's findings of no significant alteration signs.

propositions.text: Officer gave no reason to disregard expert's findings about absence of significant alteration signs.
propositions.quote: the officer did not provide any reason to disregard the expert’s findings regarding the absence of significant signs of alteration.

propositions.text: Officer alleged date of birth was erased and corrected, but CBSA analyst made same observation without mentioning it in report.
propositions.quote: She merely alleged that the date of birth was erased and corrected on the original document and drew her own conclusions. However, the CBSA’s counterfeit analyst was able to make this same observation and did not mention it in his report.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer ignored expert findings and drew unsupported conclusions about date of birth alteration.

propositions.text: Officer failed to mention two affidavits confirming applicant's identity and including a photo.
propositions.quote: the officer failed to mention in her decision two (2) affidavits produced by the applicant: her sister’s affidavit and that of a friend who knew her both in Burundi and Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer failed to mention two affidavits confirming the applicant's identity.

propositions.text: Officer breached procedural fairness by not informing applicant of concerns about identity card authenticity.
propositions.quote: the officer should have informed the applicant of her concerns about the authenticity of her national identity card. In failing to do so, she breached her duty of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Officer's decision is unreasonable as shown above; judicial review application allowed and matter referred for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: Her decision is also unreasonable as shown in the paragraphs above. For these reasons, the application for judicial review must be allowed and the matter referred to another officer for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the officer breached procedural fairness and made an unreasonable decision; judicial review allowed and case referred.

propositions.text: Applicant proposes certifying several questions.
propositions.quote: The applicant proposes that the Court certify several questions.

propositions.text: Respondent opposes certification of questions.
propositions.quote: The defendant is opposed.

propositions.text: No need to certify questions as ruling on other arguments is unnecessary, citing precedents.
propositions.quote: Given that the Court finds that it is not necessary to rule on the other arguments raised by the applicant, there is no need to certify the questions (Zhang v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FCA 168 at para. 9; Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Zazai, 2004 FCA 89 at para. 12; Pierre v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1249 at paras. 46-47).

propositions.text: Judgment: judicial review allowed; no question certified; decision set aside; case referred for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review be allowed; No question is certified. 2. The decision rendered on July 20, 2016, is set aside and the case is referred to another immigration officer for reconsideration of the application;

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks question certification; respondent opposes; court denies certification and allows judicial review, setting aside decision and referring case.
